title: Towards Quantum Network Performance Metrics: Challenges and Demonstration
authors: Mohamed Shaban, Mariam Kiran, Muhammad Ismail
abstract: As quantum networks move toward practical deployment, standardized performance monitoring becomes essential. This article proposes a structured monitoring framework for quantum networks with performance metrics, including quality (e.g., entanglement fidelity, QBER, loss, dark count rate), throughput and latency (e.g., entanglement rate, waiting time), timing (e.g., coincidence window, production and coincidence jitter), and exogenous factors (e.g., temperature, humidity, vibrations). These measurements enable real-time observability, benchmarking, and control, supporting use cases such as fault diagnosis, adaptive timing, and entanglement routing. Additionally, we implement a non-invasive prototype environmental monitoring system integrated with the quantum network infrastructure at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, demonstrating practical feasibility of live data collection and alert generation. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges of real-time monitoring and the trade-offs between observability and system performance. This work establishes a foundation for developing advanced quantum network monitoring systems and lays the groundwork for future autonomous control and quantum software-defined networking.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive monitoring framework essential for making quantum networks practical. It defines metrics covering state quality (fidelity, QBER), data rates, timing jitter, and environmental factors. By demonstrating an integrated prototype, the authors lay the groundwork for autonomous control systems in future quantum internet infrastructure.
main_problem: Standardized, comprehensive performance monitoring is necessary for quantum networks to move from research prototypes to practical deployment.
main_result: The authors propose a structured framework encompassing quality, throughput/latency, timing, and environmental metrics, validated by an integrated prototype system.
method: They define specific metrics (e.g., fidelity, QBER) and implement a physical monitoring system using off-the-shelf components to collect both quantum and classical environmental data in real time.
model_or_system: The work focuses on the operational quantum network infrastructure at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), which uses entangled photon pairs generated via crystals for demonstration. The framework integrates this with external sensors (temperature, humidity) monitored by a Prometheus/Grafana stack.
key_observables: Entanglement fidelity ($F$), Quantum Bit Error Rate ($	ext{QBER}$), entanglement rate, link loss, dark count rate, coincidence jitter, temperature, and humidity.
important_parameters: The trade-off between detailed observability overhead and maintaining high system performance is a critical parameter space explored. Sub-nanosecond timing synchronization accuracy is also key.
main_assumptions: It assumes that monitoring can be performed non-invasively without significantly degrading the quantum state or introducing excessive classical communication load.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates common metrics from classical networks (perfSONAR); Figure 2 shows the ORNL quantum local area network setup involving Alice, Bob, and Charlie.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for standardized monitoring, details the comprehensive set of required metrics across four categories, presents an environmental monitoring prototype implementation, discusses diagnostic capabilities, and concludes by outlining challenges like overhead and control complexity.
why_interesting: It provides a blueprint for operationalizing quantum hardware by treating system performance as a measurable engineering problem, which is crucial for scaling up any quantum technology.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Monitoring in a classical network, showing a three- node topology instrumented with perfSONAR hosts (PS1 and PS2) to collect active measurement data, where NetFlow and SNMP denote flow-level traffic records exported by network devices and device/interface statistics, respectively.

Figure 2: Illustration of the ORNL quantum local area network, spanning three interconnected quantum nodes labeled Alice, Bob, and Charlie. The central diagram illustrates the architectural layout and major components of each node. A zoomed-in laboratory image highlights the physical quantum optics setup at one site. Each laboratory includes a prototype monitoring system based on a Raspberry Pi 5 connected to an SHT35 digital sensor. These systems currently collect real-time temperature and humidity data, which are pushed to a Prometheus database and visualized on a Grafana dashboard.

Figure 3: Illustration of timing metrics in quantum networks, showing an entanglement source emitting multiple photon pairs, each pair encoded with a distinct color to differentiate them, as they travel toward two detectors. This visualization highlights the differences between production jitter, coinci- dence jitter, and the coincidence window. Production jitter represents the variability in emission times between consecutive photon pairs. The coincidence window is the allowable time in- terval within which detection events are considered to originate from the same entangled pair.
